passages.q: If intelligent life is likely elsewhere, why have we found no sign of it?
p: During a lunchtime conversation at Los Alamos in 1950, the physicist Enrico Fermi is said to have asked where everybody was, and the question has given its name to a puzzle: the galaxy contains hundreds of billions of stars, many with planets in habitable zones, and it is billions of years older than the Earth, so that even a civilisation expanding slowly could, in principle, have spread across it many times over, yet we observe no unambiguous trace of anyone.

Proposed resolutions fall into broad families. Perhaps life, or intelligent life, is far rarer than simple counts of planets suggest, because one or more steps, such as the origin of life, the emergence of complex cells or the development of technology, are extraordinarily improbable, a bottleneck sometimes called the great filter. Perhaps civilisations are common but short-lived, destroying themselves before they spread. Perhaps they exist but are too distant, too quiet or too different for our methods to detect, and our search has so far examined only a minute fraction of possible signals.

The puzzle is unusual in that its possible answers bear on our own prospects. If the filter lies behind us, at the origin of life for instance, humanity may be rare but has already passed the hardest test; if it lies ahead, the silence of the galaxy may be a warning. Absent evidence, the honest position is uncertainty, which is why astronomers continue to search for chemical signs of life in the atmospheres of distant planets, a search whose results, positive or negative, would be among the most consequential in history.
g: Fermi asked where everyone is, because the old, vast galaxy should allow civilisations to spread, yet we see no trace.
Explanations include a great filter making intelligence rare, short-lived civilisations, or civilisations we cannot detect with our limited search.
Where the filter lies matters for our future, so with no evidence the honest stance is uncertainty, and the search continues.
k: The Fermi paradox: a vast, old galaxy should show signs of civilisations, but we see none.
Explanations: a great filter (rare life or intelligence), self-destruction, or our detection limits.
If the filter is ahead, silence is a warning; uncertainty drives continued searches for biosignatures.

passages.t: The statistics that convicted an innocent mother
passages.q: How can a misused probability lead a court to the wrong verdict?
p: In 1999 Sally Clark, a solicitor in England, was convicted of murdering her two infant sons, who had died suddenly in separate incidents. A prominent paediatrician testified that the chance of two children in an affluent family dying of sudden infant death syndrome was about one in seventy-three million, a figure obtained by squaring the estimated chance of a single such death, and the number appeared to make innocent explanations all but impossible.

The reasoning contained two serious errors. Squaring assumed that the deaths were independent, when genetic or environmental factors shared within a family may make a second death far more likely once a first has occurred. More fundamentally, the figure invited the court to commit what statisticians call the prosecutor’s fallacy: confusing the probability of the evidence given innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence. Double murder by a mother is also extraordinarily rare, and the relevant question is which rare explanation is more likely, not how rare one of them is in isolation. The Royal Statistical Society publicly criticised the statistic.

Clark’s conviction was overturned on appeal in 2003, after it emerged that evidence of an infection in one child had not been disclosed, and other cases involving the same expert were reviewed. She died in 2007. The case is now taught as a warning that impressive numbers can mislead decision-makers who lack the training to interrogate them, and that in any setting, from courts to boardrooms, a probability must always be asked: compared with what?
g: Sally Clark was convicted partly on a claimed one-in-73-million chance of two cot deaths, which made innocence seem impossible.
The figure wrongly assumed independence and invited the prosecutor’s fallacy, ignoring that double murder is also very rare, as statisticians protested.
Her conviction was overturned in 2003, and the case warns that probabilities must always be compared with alternatives.
k: Sally Clark was convicted partly on a ‘1 in 73 million’ claim about two cot deaths.
Errors: assuming independence and the prosecutor’s fallacy; double murder is also extremely rare.
Overturned in 2003; always ask of a probability: compared with what?

passages.q: How did a bacterial defence system become a precise tool for editing genes?
p: Bacteria are constantly attacked by viruses, and many have evolved a remarkable defence: they store fragments of viral DNA in their own genome, in repeating regions known as CRISPR, and use them as templates to guide a protein, Cas9 in the best-studied system, to recognise and cut matching viral DNA if the same virus returns. The system is, in effect, a molecular memory of past infections combined with a programmable pair of scissors.

In 2012 the biochemists Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that the guiding component could be replaced with a custom-designed RNA sequence, so that Cas9 would cut DNA at almost any chosen location. Because cells repair such cuts, sometimes imprecisely and sometimes by copying a supplied template, researchers could disable genes or insert changes far more easily and cheaply than with earlier techniques. Doudna and Charpentier received the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 2020, and the method spread to thousands of laboratories within a few years.

Applications range from crop breeding to medicine: in 2023 regulators in Britain and the United States approved the first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease and a related blood disorder, which edits patients’ own blood stem cells outside the body. The technique also raises unresolved concerns, including unintended edits elsewhere in the genome and, above all, the ethics of altering embryos in ways that would be inherited, a line crossed in 2018 by a researcher in China who was subsequently imprisoned. The power to rewrite genes has outpaced agreement on when it should be used.
g: Bacteria store viral DNA in CRISPR regions to guide Cas9 to cut returning viruses, a memory plus programmable scissors.
Doudna and Charpentier showed a custom guide lets Cas9 cut almost anywhere, so gene editing became easy and cheap, winning a 2020 Nobel.
It led to the first approved therapy in 2023, but off-target edits and inherited embryo editing raise unresolved ethical concerns.
k: CRISPR-Cas9 is a bacterial immune memory that cuts matching viral DNA.
Doudna and Charpentier (2012) made it programmable to cut almost any DNA; Nobel 2020.

passages.q: Is war likely when a rising power challenges an established one?
p: The ancient Greek historian Thucydides wrote that what made the Peloponnesian War inevitable was the growth of Athenian power and the fear this caused in Sparta, and the political scientist Graham Allison, in his 2017 book Destined for War, used the phrase Thucydides’s trap for the dangerous dynamic that arises when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one; his team examined sixteen such cases over five centuries and reported that twelve ended in war.

The framework has been widely applied to relations between the United States and China, and its appeal lies in its structural argument: even leaders who do not want war may be driven towards it by fear, miscalculation and the escalating logic of each side’s attempts to secure its position, which the other interprets as aggression. Allison insisted that war was not inevitable and cited cases, such as the peaceful transition from British to American pre-eminence in the twentieth century, in which it was avoided.

Critics have questioned the case selection, arguing that the definition of a rising and ruling power is elastic and that some wars on the list had other primary causes; others note that nuclear weapons and economic interdependence make modern great-power war unlike earlier conflicts. The concept is perhaps best read not as a prediction but as a warning about how structural pressures can overwhelm intentions, which is why the cases in which war was avoided, and the deliberate choices that made the difference, deserve as much study as those in which it was not.
g: Allison named Thucydides’s trap after the historian’s claim that Athens’ rise and Sparta’s fear made war inevitable, finding war in 12 of 16 cases.
It is applied to the US and China because fear and miscalculation can drive unwilling leaders to war, though Allison said war is avoidable.
Critics question case selection and note nuclear and economic differences, so it is best read as a warning, studying cases where war was avoided.
k: Thucydides’s trap: a rising power and a fearful ruling power; Allison found war in 12 of 16 cases.
Structural fear and miscalculation can drive unwilling leaders to war; Allison says it is avoidable.

passages.t: Goods that sell more when they cost more
passages.q: Why does demand for some luxury goods rise with their price?
p: The ordinary law of demand holds that as the price of a good rises, people buy less of it, and most purchases bear this out; yet the economist and sociologist Thorstein Veblen observed in his 1899 book The Theory of the Leisure Class that for certain goods, display was part of the point, so that their high price, by signalling wealth and status, made them more desirable rather than less, a phenomenon he called conspicuous consumption.

Goods whose appeal depends partly on their expense are now known as Veblen goods, and luxury brands manage them with great care. Discounts that would boost sales of ordinary products can damage a luxury brand by eroding exclusivity, which is why some houses have historically destroyed unsold stock rather than mark it down, a practice that drew public criticism and, in France, legislation. Prices may be raised deliberately, and supply is often restricted, as with waiting lists for certain watches or handbags, so that scarcity itself becomes a signal.

Veblen effects coexist with ordinary demand rather than replacing it: beyond some point, even luxury buyers balk, and the signalling value of a brand can collapse if it becomes associated with the wrong buyers or loses its aura. The deeper point is that price communicates as well as rations, and that for products bought partly to say something about the buyer, managing what the price says can matter as much as managing what it costs.
g: Normally higher prices reduce demand, but Veblen noticed that for display goods high prices signal status and raise desirability.
Luxury brands protect these Veblen goods by avoiding discounts, even destroying stock, raising prices and restricting supply so scarcity signals.
Ordinary demand still applies at extremes and signals can collapse, but price communicates as well as rations, so managing its message matters.
k: Veblen (1899): for some goods, a high price signals status and increases demand.
Luxury brands avoid discounts, restrict supply and raise prices to protect exclusivity.

passages.q: Can any voting system turn individual preferences into a fair group choice?
p: As far back as the eighteenth century, the Marquis de Condorcet noticed that majority voting could produce cycles: a group might prefer option A to B and B to C by majority, yet also prefer C to A, so that no option beats all others and the outcome depends on the order in which choices are put. In 1951 the economist Kenneth Arrow proved a far more general result, showing that the problem cannot be engineered away.

Arrow listed a handful of conditions that seem essential to any fair method of combining individual rankings of three or more options into a group ranking: if everyone prefers one option to another, so should the group; the group’s ranking of two options should depend only on how individuals rank those two, not on irrelevant alternatives; and no single individual should dictate the outcome. He proved that no ranked voting system can satisfy all these conditions at once. Arrow received the Nobel Prize in economics in 1972, partly for this impossibility theorem.

The theorem does not imply that democracy is futile or that all voting systems are equally good; it means that every system involves trade-offs, so that choices between first-past-the-post, ranked-choice or other methods are choices between kinds of imperfection. It also explains why agenda-setting, the power to decide which options are considered and in what order, can be so influential in committees and legislatures, since where preferences cycle, whoever controls the sequence may effectively control the result.
g: Condorcet saw majority voting can cycle so outcomes depend on order, and Arrow proved in 1951 this cannot be engineered away.
Arrow showed no ranked voting system can meet a short list of seemingly essential fairness conditions at once, winning a Nobel.
So every system trades off imperfections, and agenda-setting becomes powerful because controlling order can control outcomes.
k: Condorcet: majority preferences can cycle (A>B, B>C, C>A).

passages.q: What makes quantum computers different from ordinary ones?
p: Popular descriptions often claim that quantum computers try every possible answer at once, which is misleading. An ordinary bit is either 0 or 1; a quantum bit, or qubit, can exist in a superposition of both, and a set of qubits can be entangled so that their states are correlated in ways that have no classical equivalent. But when the qubits are measured, the computation yields a single result, and a quantum algorithm is useful only if it arranges for wrong answers to cancel out and right answers to reinforce, through a process called interference.

Such algorithms exist for only certain problems. Peter Shor showed in 1994 that a sufficiently large quantum computer could factor large numbers exponentially faster than any known classical method, which would break widely used encryption, and quantum computers are expected to excel at simulating molecules and materials, which are themselves quantum systems. For many everyday tasks, by contrast, there is no known quantum advantage, and a quantum computer would offer nothing over a laptop.

The engineering obstacles are formidable. Qubits are extraordinarily fragile, losing their quantum properties through interactions with their surroundings, so useful machines will need error correction that combines many physical qubits into each reliable logical qubit, potentially requiring millions of physical qubits for applications such as breaking encryption. Progress has been rapid but uneven, and governments are already migrating to encryption designed to resist quantum attack, on the reasoning that data stolen today could be decrypted once such machines exist.
g: Quantum computers do not try all answers at once; qubits use superposition and entanglement, and algorithms use interference to favour right answers.
This helps only certain problems, like Shor’s factoring and molecular simulation, and offers no advantage for most everyday tasks.
Fragile qubits need error correction with possibly millions of physical qubits, so governments are already moving to quantum-resistant encryption.

passages.q: Why do people judge two choices with the same outcome so differently?
p: In a thought experiment introduced by the philosopher Philippa Foot in 1967 and developed by Judith Jarvis Thomson, a runaway trolley will kill five workers unless you pull a lever diverting it onto a side track, where it will kill one; most people say that pulling the lever is permissible. But when the scenario is changed so that the only way to stop the trolley is to push a large man off a footbridge into its path, killing him but saving the five, most people say that doing so would be wrong, even though the arithmetic of lives is identical.

Philosophers have proposed principles to explain the difference, such as the distinction between harm that is a side effect of an action and harm that is used as a means to an end, or between redirecting an existing threat and initiating a new one. Psychologists, including Joshua Greene, have argued from brain-imaging and behavioural studies that the personal, physical character of pushing triggers an emotional response that overrides utilitarian calculation, whereas pulling a lever, being impersonal, leaves room for counting lives.

The scenarios are artificial, and critics doubt that responses to stylised puzzles reveal much about real moral life. Yet they have acquired practical relevance in debates about autonomous vehicles and military systems, where designers must decide in advance how machines should trade off harms. Perhaps their most useful lesson is that moral intuitions are sensitive to features, such as physical contact and intention, that we may or may not endorse on reflection, so that deciding which distinctions truly matter requires argument rather than reliance on gut reactions alone.
g: Most people would pull a lever to divert a trolley killing one to save five, but would not push a man off a bridge, despite identical numbers.

passages.t: Why safe banks can collapse overnight
passages.q: How can a solvent bank fail simply because depositors panic?
p: Banks perform a valuable transformation: they take deposits that customers can withdraw at any time and lend them out as long-term loans, such as mortgages, that cannot quickly be recalled. In a 1983 model, the economists Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig showed that this transformation, which allows savers to earn returns while retaining access to their money, also creates a fragility: if enough depositors fear that others will withdraw first, it becomes rational for each to withdraw immediately, and the bank, unable to sell its long-term assets quickly without heavy losses, may fail even if it was solvent, with assets worth more than its debts.

The run is self-fulfilling, since the belief that a bank will fail is enough to make it fail. Diamond and Dybvig showed that deposit insurance, by guaranteeing depositors their money regardless of what others do, can remove the incentive to run without ever needing to be paid out, and central banks acting as lenders of last resort serve a similar function. Diamond and Dybvig shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in economics with Ben Bernanke, who had studied how bank failures deepened the Great Depression.

The collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023 showed the old mechanism operating at digital speed. Much of its deposit base, drawn from technology firms, exceeded the insured limit, and when losses on its bond holdings became public, depositors coordinated through messaging apps and withdrew tens of billions of dollars in a single day. The episode prompted debate about whether deposit guarantees should be extended, and about how regulators should account for the speed at which modern runs can now unfold.
g: Banks turn instant-access deposits into long-term loans, and Diamond and Dybvig showed this lets fear trigger runs that sink sound banks.
Runs are self-fulfilling, so deposit insurance and lenders of last resort can stop them without paying out, earning a 2022 Nobel.
Silicon Valley Bank’s 2023 collapse showed runs now happen at digital speed, prompting debate on guarantees and regulation.

passages.t: What a language model actually does
passages.q: How does a system trained to predict the next word come to appear so capable?
p: Large language models are trained on an apparently modest task: given a sequence of text, predict the next fragment, called a token, which may be a word or part of one. During training, the model sees vast quantities of text and adjusts billions of internal parameters to make its predictions slightly better each time, and when deployed, it generates responses by repeatedly predicting a likely next token and appending it to the text so far.

The simplicity of the objective conceals its difficulty. To predict the next word of a physics textbook, a legal argument or a piece of computer code reliably, a model benefits from representing something about the concepts, relationships and reasoning patterns the text expresses, and as models and datasets have grown, they have exhibited abilities, such as translation, summarisation and multi-step problem-solving, that were not explicitly programmed. Developers then refine the raw models with further training, including human feedback, to make them more helpful and to reduce harmful outputs.

The same mechanism explains characteristic weaknesses. Because a model produces plausible continuations, it can state falsehoods fluently, a failure often called hallucination, and its outputs reflect patterns, including biases, in its training data. Researchers disagree about how far such systems understand what they process, and about how quickly their capabilities will continue to grow. For users, a practical stance follows from the mechanism: treat outputs as drafts that may be impressively right or confidently wrong, and verify claims that matter.
g: Language models are trained to predict the next token and generate text by repeating that prediction.

passages.q: Why do upheavals often follow improvement rather than misery?
p: Writing in 1856 about the origins of the French Revolution, the political thinker Alexis de Tocqueville noted a paradox: the parts of France where conditions had improved most in the decades before 1789 were often those where discontent was greatest, and he concluded that the most dangerous moment for a bad government is usually when it begins to reform, because evils that were patiently endured when they seemed beyond remedy become intolerable once people glimpse the possibility of escape.

Later social scientists developed related ideas. The sociologist James Davies proposed in 1962 that revolutions are most likely when a long period of rising expectations and improving conditions is followed by a sharp reversal, so that the gap between what people expect and what they get suddenly widens. Theories of relative deprivation similarly emphasise that people judge their situation against expectations and comparison groups rather than absolute standards.

The insight has applications well beyond revolutions. Organisations undergoing reform often experience their sharpest internal dissent not in the long period of stagnation but when change begins, because hopes rise faster than results; customers who have been promised improvements are more aggrieved by a minor failure than those who expected nothing. Leaders managing change are therefore wise to manage expectations as carefully as conditions, since satisfaction depends on the relationship between the two.
g: Tocqueville noticed the most improved parts of pre-revolutionary France were often the most discontented, because reform makes endured evils seem escapable.
Davies argued revolutions follow rising expectations then sharp reversals, and relative deprivation theory says people judge against expectations.

passages.q: Why should investors and planners build in a margin of safety?
p: The investor Benjamin Graham, in his 1949 book The Intelligent Investor, argued that the central concept of sound investment could be summed up in three words, margin of safety: an investor should buy a security only when its price is substantially below a conservative estimate of its intrinsic value, so that even if the estimate proves optimistic, or events turn out worse than expected, the investment is still unlikely to produce a severe loss.

The idea borrows from engineering, where a bridge designed to carry ten tonnes is built to withstand far more, because loads, materials and models are all uncertain. Graham’s insight was that valuation is equally uncertain: forecasts of earnings, growth and interest rates are estimates, and an investor who pays full value for a perfect forecast has no protection against the forecast being wrong. The margin is not a prediction of disaster but an admission that one’s analysis may be mistaken in ways one cannot foresee.

The principle extends to planning of every kind. A project scheduled to finish exactly on its deadline if everything goes right will almost certainly be late; a company that borrows to the limit of what it can service in a good year may not survive a bad one; a presenter who rehearses until the talk just fits the slot has no time to recover from an interruption. Margins look wasteful in good times, which is precisely when they are most often eroded, and indispensable in bad times, when it is too late to create them.
g: Graham said sound investing needs a margin of safety: buy well below a conservative value estimate to limit losses if wrong.
Like engineers overbuilding bridges, investors face uncertain forecasts, so the margin admits analysis may be mistaken.
The principle applies to schedules, borrowing and rehearsal, and margins look wasteful in good times yet are vital in bad ones.
k: Graham’s margin of safety: buy well below a conservative estimate of intrinsic value.
Like engineering safety factors, it admits forecasts and analysis may be wrong.

passages.q: How can teams tell metrics that guide decisions from metrics that merely look good?
p: In The Lean Startup, published in 2011, the entrepreneur Eric Ries distinguished between vanity metrics, such as total registered users, cumulative downloads or page views, which tend to rise over time regardless of whether a product is improving and which make teams feel successful, and actionable metrics, which tie specific changes to specific outcomes clearly enough to inform the next decision.

Cumulative totals almost never fall, so they cannot reveal whether last month’s changes helped; a company can add users every week while the proportion who return after their first visit steadily declines. Actionable alternatives include cohort analysis, which tracks groups of users who joined at the same time and compares their behaviour, and controlled experiments, in which a change is shown to some users and not others. Such measures are less flattering and often more alarming, which is exactly what makes them useful.

The distinction is not only about which numbers are collected but about what they are used for. Any metric can become a vanity metric if it is reported to celebrate rather than to decide, and any can be actionable if it is linked to a hypothesis about cause and effect. A good test for a dashboard is to ask, for each figure, what the team would do differently if it moved sharply in either direction; numbers for which the answer is nothing are decoration rather than instruments.
g: Ries distinguished vanity metrics, which rise regardless and flatter teams, from actionable metrics that link changes to outcomes.
Totals rarely fall and hide declining engagement, so cohort analysis and experiments, though less flattering, are more useful.
What matters is use, so for each dashboard figure ask what you would do if it moved; if nothing, it is decoration.
k: Vanity metrics (totals, downloads, page views) rise regardless and flatter; actionable metrics inform decisions.
Cumulative totals hide decline; cohorts and controlled experiments reveal cause and effect.
Ask what you’d do if each metric moved sharply; if nothing, it’s decoration.

passages.q: Why can a small initial warming lead to a larger one?
p: Adding carbon dioxide to the atmosphere traps heat directly, but the warming that results from this direct effect alone would be relatively modest; much of the expected warming comes from feedbacks, processes in which an initial change triggers responses that amplify or dampen it. Understanding these feedbacks, and their uncertainties, is central to estimating how sensitive the climate is to greenhouse gases.

Several amplifying feedbacks are well established. Warmer air holds more water vapour, itself a powerful greenhouse gas, so warming increases humidity, which causes further warming. Ice and snow reflect most incoming sunlight, so as they melt, darker ocean and land beneath absorb more energy, accelerating warming, particularly in the Arctic, which is heating several times faster than the global average. In some regions, thawing permafrost may release stored carbon as carbon dioxide and methane. Clouds can act in either direction, cooling by reflecting sunlight or warming by trapping heat, and they remain a major source of uncertainty in projections.

Feedbacks explain why scientists speak of climate sensitivity, the long-term warming expected from a doubling of carbon dioxide, as a range rather than a single number; recent assessments place the likely value at roughly two and a half to four degrees Celsius. They also underlie concern about tipping points, thresholds beyond which a feedback becomes self-sustaining and a change, such as the loss of a major ice sheet, becomes effectively irreversible on human timescales, even if emissions later fall.
g: Carbon dioxide’s direct warming is modest, and much warming comes from feedbacks that amplify or dampen it.
Amplifiers include water vapour, melting ice and thawing permafrost, while clouds work either way and remain uncertain.
So climate sensitivity is a range of about 2.5–4°C, and feedbacks raise the risk of irreversible tipping points.
k: Much expected warming comes from feedbacks, not CO₂’s direct effect alone.
Amplifiers: water vapour, ice–albedo, permafrost; clouds are a major uncertainty.
Sensitivity to doubled CO₂ is likely about 2.5–4°C; tipping points may make changes irreversible.

passages.q: Do market prices simply reflect reality, or can they change it?
p: Standard economic theory treats prices as tending towards an equilibrium determined by underlying fundamentals, such as a company’s future profits or a country’s economic strength, with market participants acting as observers who try to estimate those fundamentals correctly. The investor George Soros argued that this picture omits something crucial, which he called reflexivity: participants’ beliefs influence prices, and prices in turn influence the fundamentals they are supposed to reflect.

A rising share price can make it easier for a company to raise capital, acquire rivals with its own stock and attract talent, improving the very performance that investors are betting on; a falling price can do the opposite. In lending booms, rising property prices increase the value of collateral, allowing more borrowing, which pushes prices higher still, until the process reverses and falling prices force sales that drive them lower. In such feedback loops, prices do not simply converge on a fixed value but can overshoot in both directions, producing booms and busts.

Mainstream economists have long recognised that expectations matter and that markets can deviate from fundamentals, and many regard reflexivity as a vivid restatement of familiar ideas rather than a new theory. Its practical value lies in the warning it gives: when a trend’s own momentum is improving the conditions that justify it, the apparent confirmation is partly circular, and the same mechanism that sustained the rise can accelerate the fall.
g: Standard theory sees prices tending to fundamentals, but Soros argued reflexivity means beliefs move prices and prices change fundamentals.

Economists see it as a restatement, but it warns that self-reinforcing trends are partly circular and can reverse sharply.
k: Soros’s reflexivity: beliefs influence prices, and prices influence the fundamentals they reflect.
Share prices and collateral values can feed back into performance and credit, causing overshooting booms and busts.

passages.t: Is it still the same company?
passages.q: What makes an organisation the same organisation when everything about it changes?
p: An ancient puzzle, recorded by Plutarch, concerns the ship of the Athenian hero Theseus, which was preserved for generations by replacing its rotting planks one at a time, until eventually none of the original timber remained; philosophers asked whether it was still the same ship, and the philosopher Thomas Hobbes later sharpened the puzzle by asking what would follow if someone collected the discarded planks and reassembled them into a second ship.

Philosophers have offered several answers, emphasising continuity of form, continuity of function, gradualness of change or the conventions by which we choose to apply names, and none commands universal agreement. The puzzle has a practical counterpart in organisations, almost all of whose components are replaced over time. A company that has changed its products, staff, owners, headquarters and even its name may still be regarded as the same company, while one that keeps its name but abandons its purpose may feel, to its employees and customers, like something else entirely.

For leaders, the question of identity is not merely academic. Decisions about what to preserve during transformation, which traditions express the organisation’s purpose and which merely reflect past circumstances, determine whether change is experienced as renewal or as loss. A useful approach is to identify what customers and employees believe the organisation fundamentally is and does, protect that through changes of form, and be willing to replace almost everything else, plank by plank.
g: The ship of Theseus, rebuilt plank by plank, asks whether it is the same ship, and Hobbes sharpened this by imagining the old planks reassembled.
Answers stress form, function, gradual change or naming conventions, and organisations face the same puzzle as everything is replaced.
Leaders must decide what to preserve, so protect what people believe the organisation fundamentally is and change the rest.
k: The ship of Theseus asks what persists when every part is replaced; Hobbes added the reassembled-planks twist.
Answers cite form, function, gradual change or convention; organisations face the same question.
Protect what people believe the organisation fundamentally is and does; replace the rest.

passages.t: What people say versus what they think
passages.q: Why do sudden social changes so often surprise everyone?
p: The economist Timur Kuran argued in his 1995 book Private Truths, Public Lies that people frequently misrepresent their genuine preferences in public, conforming to what they believe others expect in order to avoid social or political penalties, a behaviour he called preference falsification. When many people conceal the same private view, each may wrongly believe that he or she is nearly alone, which reinforces the silence.

Because individuals differ in how much pressure they need before they will speak openly, a society can harbour widespread but hidden dissent that appears stable on the surface. If a few people with low thresholds speak out, others discover that their private views are shared, which lowers the cost of speaking for those with slightly higher thresholds, and a cascade can follow. Kuran used this mechanism to explain why the collapse of communist regimes in Eastern Europe in 1989 surprised nearly everyone, including the participants: the preferences that drove it had been invisible until they suddenly were not.

The theory implies that public opinion can be a poor guide to private opinion where the costs of dissent are high, and that apparent consensus may be fragile. Its implications extend to workplaces, where surveys that are not truly anonymous and meetings dominated by senior voices may reveal what people feel safe saying rather than what they think. Leaders who want accurate information must lower the cost of candour, or they will be among the last to learn what their own organisations believe.
g: Kuran argued people hide their real preferences to avoid penalties, and each may think they are alone, reinforcing silence.
Differing thresholds mean hidden dissent can cascade once a few speak, explaining the surprise collapse of communism in 1989.
So public opinion can mislead and consensus can be fragile, and leaders must lower the cost of candour to learn the truth.
k: Preference falsification: people publicly conform while privately disagreeing (Kuran, 1995).

passages.q: How can sensible individuals collectively make a poor choice?
p: Imagine diners choosing between two unfamiliar restaurants side by side. The first diner has a slight private reason to prefer A and goes there; the second also privately leans slightly towards B, but seeing someone in A, reasonably infers that the first diner knew something, and follows; a third, seeing two people in A, is even more inclined to follow, and soon everyone eats at A, even if most of them had private information favouring B. Economists including Sushil Bikhchandani, David Hirshleifer and Ivo Welch described this dynamic in 1992 as an information cascade.

In a cascade, each individual acts rationally given what they observe, but once people begin to follow others rather than their own information, their choices stop revealing what they privately know, so the crowd’s behaviour contains less information than it appears to. A cascade can therefore rest on very little evidence, the choices of the first few people, and be fragile: a small piece of new public information can reverse it suddenly, which helps explain fads, sudden shifts in fashion, bank runs and rapid swings in the popularity of products.

The mechanism matters for organisations because many decisions are made sequentially and publicly, with later speakers influenced by earlier ones. Hiring panels in which members announce opinions in order of seniority, investment committees where the first view sets the tone, and product reviews that begin with a few early ratings are all vulnerable. Asking people to record independent judgements before they hear others’ restores the information that a cascade would otherwise discard.
g: Diners following others into restaurant A, despite private leanings to B, illustrate an information cascade.
Each acts rationally but stops revealing private information, so cascades rest on little evidence and can reverse suddenly, explaining fads and runs.
Sequential public decisions in panels, committees and reviews are vulnerable, so record independent judgements first.
k: Information cascades: people rationally follow earlier choices, ignoring their own information.
Cascades carry little real information, rest on early choices and can reverse suddenly (fads, runs).
Collect independent judgements before discussion to preserve information.

passages.t: Designing the rules of the game
passages.q: How can a well-designed auction serve both sellers and society?
p: When governments began selling licences to use radio spectrum for mobile phones, they faced a design problem: licences for different regions and frequencies were worth more in combination than separately, bidders held different private information about their value, and a poorly designed sale could leave licences with the wrong owners or raise far less money than it should. The economists Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson, who shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in economics, developed auction formats, notably the simultaneous multiple-round auction, in which many related licences are sold at the same time over successive rounds, allowing bidders to learn from each other’s bids and assemble sensible combinations.

The field to which they contributed, mechanism design, inverts the usual question in economics: rather than predicting how people will behave under given rules, it asks what rules will lead self-interested participants, each with private information, to produce a desired outcome. Auction formats can be designed to reduce the winner’s curse by revealing information as bidding proceeds, to deter collusion and to encourage participants to bid what licences are truly worth to them.

Results have been dramatic. Britain’s 2000 auction of third-generation mobile licences raised around twenty-two billion pounds, far more than expected, while some poorly designed auctions elsewhere raised little or collapsed amid collusion. Revenue is not the only goal, however, since governments also want licences to go to firms that will use them well and competitively, and a sale that extracts too much may leave winners burdened with debt. The deeper lesson is that rules shape outcomes, and that designing them well is a technical discipline with real economic consequences.
g: Spectrum licences were worth more in combination and bidders had private information, so Milgrom and Wilson designed simultaneous multi-round auctions.
Mechanism design asks which rules lead self-interested people to good outcomes, such as auctions that reveal information and deter collusion.

passages.q: Why might an extra pound be worth more to some people than to others?
p: The principle of diminishing marginal utility holds that the additional satisfaction a person gains from one more unit of something tends to fall as they have more of it: a first meal for a hungry person is invaluable, a fifth in the same day is worth little. Applied to money, the principle implies that a hundred pounds means far more to someone with very little than to someone who is already rich, a conclusion supported by research finding that life satisfaction rises roughly with the logarithm of income, so that each doubling of income is associated with a similar gain.

This idea has long been used to argue for progressive taxation and for redistribution: if money is worth less at the margin to the rich, transferring some of it to the poor could increase total well-being. The economist Arthur Pigou made such arguments in the early twentieth century, and versions of them underlie modern tax and benefit systems in which rates rise with income.

The argument faces serious objections. Comparing satisfaction between different people is philosophically contested, since we cannot directly measure one person’s happiness against another’s. High taxes may reduce incentives to work, invest or innovate, shrinking the total available. And people may regard what they have earned as rightfully theirs, so that fairness is not reducible to totals of well-being. The principle of diminishing marginal utility is widely accepted; how much weight it should carry in policy, against these other considerations, is a question of values as much as economics.
g: Diminishing marginal utility means each extra unit adds less satisfaction, so £100 matters more to the poor, as log-income research suggests.
This has long supported progressive taxes and redistribution, as Pigou argued, because transfers could raise total well-being.
Objections include comparing happiness across people, incentives and desert, so how far the principle guides policy is about values.

passages.q: Why do organisations sometimes fill senior roles with people unsuited to them?
p: In their satirical 1969 book The Peter Principle, Laurence Peter and Raymond Hull proposed that in a hierarchy every employee tends to rise to their level of incompetence: people who perform well are promoted, and they continue to be promoted until they reach a role in which they no longer perform well, where they remain, so that over time many positions are filled by people who are not good at them.

The book was written as humour, but research has found evidence for a version of the effect. A 2018 study by Alan Benson, Danielle Li and Kelly Shue, examining sales workers in many firms, found that the best salespeople were more likely to be promoted to manager, yet their teams performed worse under them than under managers who had been less outstanding salespeople, suggesting that firms were promoting on the basis of performance in the current job rather than aptitude for the next one, which requires different skills.

Organisations can reduce the problem in several ways: assessing candidates for the skills the new role actually requires, giving people trial assignments before permanent promotion, and creating career paths that reward excellent individual contributors with status and pay without forcing them into management. The underlying lesson is that past performance predicts future performance mainly when the work stays the same, and that a promotion is, in effect, a new job for which the evidence is often thin.

passages.q: Why do budgets grow, and can starting from zero stop them?
p: Most organisations set budgets incrementally: each department begins with last year’s allocation and argues about adjustments at the margin, a few per cent up or down. The approach is efficient, since it avoids re-examining everything every year, but it entrenches past decisions, so that spending justified by circumstances long gone persists simply because it was there before, and departments learn to spend their full allocation to avoid losing it.

Zero-based budgeting, developed by the manager Peter Pyhrr at Texas Instruments around 1970 and later adopted by the state of Georgia under Jimmy Carter, requires every activity to be justified from scratch as though it were new, ranked by value and funded in order of priority until the money runs out. In the 2010s it was revived by several consumer goods companies associated with the investment firm 3G Capital, which used it to make substantial cuts in overhead costs.

Critics note that the method is labour-intensive, that it can encourage short-term cost cutting at the expense of investments whose benefits are hard to quantify, such as brand building or research, and that some companies that used it aggressively later struggled to grow. Many organisations now apply its logic selectively, rebuilding particular cost categories from zero every few years rather than the whole budget annually. The principle remains useful: occasionally asking why each activity exists, not just how much it should change, exposes spending that habit has protected.

passages.q: Why do people who understand something well often struggle to explain it?
p: In a 1990 experiment at Stanford, the psychology student Elizabeth Newton asked participants to tap out the rhythm of well-known songs on a table while listeners tried to identify them. Before starting, tappers predicted that listeners would recognise about half the songs; in fact, listeners identified only about one in forty. The tappers could hear the melody in their heads as they tapped and found it hard to imagine experiencing the taps without it.

The phenomenon, often called the curse of knowledge, describes the difficulty of imagining what it is like not to know something one knows. Once we understand a concept, a piece of jargon or the context of a decision, we unconsciously assume that others share that understanding, so we skip steps, use undefined terms and present conclusions without the reasoning that made them obvious to us. Experts are especially vulnerable, which is why technical explanations so often fail their intended audiences.

Countermeasures are practical rather than mysterious. Concrete examples and stories carry meaning without requiring shared background; testing an explanation on someone outside the field reveals the gaps the expert cannot see; and asking the audience to restate the point in their own words shows whether it has landed. For anyone presenting to executives, the curse suggests a sobering rule: what feels obvious to you after weeks of analysis is the least likely part of your message to be obvious to them.
g: In Newton’s experiment, tappers expected half their songs to be guessed, but listeners got about one in forty.

So use concrete examples, test on outsiders and ask for restatements, since what feels obvious to you is least obvious to others.

passages.q: When dissatisfied, should people leave or speak up, and what does each do for an organisation?
p: In his 1970 book Exit, Voice, and Loyalty, the economist Albert Hirschman observed that when the quality of a firm, organisation or state declines, its members or customers have two broad responses: exit, leaving for an alternative, and voice, expressing dissatisfaction in the hope of bringing about improvement. Economics had focused on exit, the mechanism of markets, while political science had focused on voice, the mechanism of participation, and Hirschman argued that each needs the other.

Exit sends a signal, falling sales or departing members, but a crude one, since it says that something is wrong without saying what, and those most likely to leave are often the most demanding and quality-conscious, precisely the people whose complaints might have driven improvement. Voice conveys richer information but is costly and depends on the expectation that it will be heard. Hirschman suggested that loyalty, an attachment that makes people reluctant to leave, can be valuable because it holds members in place long enough for voice to work, though loyalty can also be exploited by organisations that take it for granted.

The framework illuminates many situations. A company that makes complaining difficult may simply lose its best customers without learning why; a public service that the wealthy can exit, by paying for private alternatives, may lose its most effective advocates for reform; an organisation whose talented staff leave quietly rather than raise concerns is receiving exit signals when it could have had voice. Leaders who want to improve should make voice cheaper and more effective, because by the time exit becomes visible, the most useful information has already walked out of the door.
g: Hirschman said declining organisations face exit or voice, which economics and political science had studied separately, and each needs the other.
Exit is a crude signal that loses the most demanding people, voice is richer but costly, and loyalty can hold people long enough for voice to work.
Hard complaining, wealthy exit and quiet departures lose information, so leaders should make voice cheap and effective.
k: Hirschman (1970): dissatisfied members can exit or use voice; both matter.

passages.t: When people change the rules you measured
passages.q: Why can policies based on past behaviour fail once they are introduced?
p: In 1976 the economist Robert Lucas published a critique of the large statistical models that governments used to forecast the effects of economic policy. Those models estimated relationships from historical data, such as how much consumption responded to income or how inflation and unemployment moved together, and assumed that the relationships would hold when policy changed. Lucas argued that this assumption was unwarranted, because the relationships themselves depend on how people expect policy to behave.

His most famous target was the apparent trade-off between inflation and unemployment, which suggested that governments could reduce unemployment by tolerating higher inflation. Once governments tried to exploit it systematically, workers and firms came to expect higher inflation and built it into wages and prices, so the trade-off disappeared, leaving higher inflation without lower unemployment, broadly the experience of several economies in the 1970s. Lucas received the Nobel Prize in economics in 1995, and his critique pushed economists to model how expectations respond to policy rules.

The principle generalises well beyond macroeconomics. Any pattern estimated from people’s past behaviour may change once they know it is being used to make decisions about them: a credit-scoring model can be gamed once its inputs are known, and a correlation between a type of customer and profitability may vanish once marketing targets them. The lesson for decision-makers is to ask not only what the data show, but how the people generating the data will respond once the decision is made.
g: Lucas criticised forecasting models in 1976 for assuming historical relationships would survive policy changes, since they depend on expectations.
The inflation-unemployment trade-off vanished once exploited, as expectations adjusted, which earned Lucas a Nobel and changed modelling.
Patterns based on past behaviour can change once used, as with gamed credit scores, so ask how people will respond.
k: Lucas critique (1976): historical relationships can break when policy changes, because expectations shift.
Exploiting the inflation–unemployment trade-off made it vanish in the 1970s; Nobel 1995.
Any behavioural pattern used for decisions may change; ask how people will respond.
